title: Power-sharing
subject: civics
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (Political Science: 20 marks). There is no map item from this chapter.

blocks.title: Two countries, two choices
blocks.body:
Belgium and Sri Lanka are both democracies, and both have people who speak different languages. In the 20th century, both faced tension between their communities.

Belgium chose to **share power** with all its groups and stayed united. Sri Lanka chose to let the **majority rule over** the minority, and slid into a long civil war. This chapter asks why sharing power is wise and right, and what forms it takes in modern democracies.

blocks.title: Power shared, not grabbed
blocks.body:
After decades of apartheid, Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first democratically elected president in **1994**. Instead of taking revenge on the white minority that had imprisoned him for 27 years, he formed a **Government of National Unity** that included leaders of the former ruling party.

By sharing power, he helped a deeply divided country move to democracy without a civil war. He showed that sharing power can protect both the minority and the majority.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in law, public administration, diplomacy, journalism and conflict resolution.

blocks.question: Why might a majority community be wise to share power with a minority?
options: Sharing power reduces conflict and keeps the country stable and united
Because the majority is always wrong
Because power sharing means no one rules
blocks.explanation: Imposing the majority's will may look attractive in the short run, but it undermines the unity of the nation in the long run.

blocks.title: Two stories of ethnic diversity
blocks.body:
**Belgium:** a small country in Europe, smaller in area than the state of Haryana. It has borders with **France, the Netherlands, Germany and Luxembourg**. It has a population of a little over one crore, about half the population of Haryana.
- **Ethnic composition:** of the country's total population, **59 per cent** lives in the **Flemish region** and speaks **Dutch**; another **40 per cent** lives in the **Wallonia region** and speaks **French**; the remaining **one per cent** speaks **German**.
- In the capital city **Brussels**, **80 per cent** speak **French**, while **20 per cent** are **Dutch**-speaking.
- The minority **French-speaking** community was relatively **rich and powerful**. This was resented by the Dutch-speaking community, who got the benefit of economic development and education much later. This led to **tensions** between the communities during the **1950s and 1960s**.
- The tension was more acute in **Brussels**: the Dutch-speaking people were a majority in the country but a **minority in the capital**.

**Sri Lanka:** an island nation, just a few kilometres off the southern coast of Tamil Nadu, with about **2 crore** people, about the same as Haryana. It has a diverse population:
- The major social groups are the **Sinhala-speakers (74 per cent)** and the **Tamil-speakers (18 per cent)**.
- Among Tamils there are two sub-groups: Tamil natives of the country, called **'Sri Lankan Tamils' (13 per cent)**; and the rest, whose forefathers came from India as **plantation workers** during the colonial period, called **'Indian Tamils'**. Sri Lankan Tamils are concentrated in the **north and east** of the country.
- Most Sinhala-speaking people are **Buddhist**, while most Tamils are **Hindus or Muslims**. There are about **7 per cent Christians**, who are both Tamil and Sinhala.

**Majoritarianism in Sri Lanka:** Sri Lanka became independent in **1948**. The leaders of the Sinhala community sought to secure dominance over the government by virtue of their majority, and the democratically elected government adopted a series of **majoritarian measures** to establish **Sinhala supremacy**:
- In **1956**, an Act was passed to recognise **Sinhala as the only official language**, disregarding Tamil.
- Governments followed **preferential policies** that favoured Sinhala applicants for **university positions and government jobs**.
- A new constitution stipulated that the state shall **protect and foster Buddhism**.

All these measures gradually increased the feeling of **alienation** among the Sri Lankan Tamils. They felt that none of the major political parties led by the Buddhist Sinhala leaders was sensitive to their language and culture, and that the constitution and government policies denied them equal political rights and discriminated against them in jobs and other opportunities.
- The Sri Lankan Tamils launched parties and struggles demanding **recognition of Tamil as an official language, regional autonomy, and equality of opportunity in securing education and jobs**. But their demand for more autonomy to provinces populated by Tamils was repeatedly denied.
- By the **1980s**, several political organisations were formed demanding an **independent Tamil Eelam (state)** in the northern and eastern parts of Sri Lanka.
- The distrust between the two communities turned into widespread conflict and soon into a **civil war**. Thousands of people of both communities were killed, many families were forced to leave the country as **refugees**, and many more lost their livelihoods. The civil war ended in **2009**.

blocks.title: Belgium and Sri Lanka compared
blocks.body:
| | Belgium | Sri Lanka |
|---|---|---|
| **Population mix** | 59% Dutch-speaking (Flemish region), 40% French-speaking (Wallonia), 1% German; Brussels 80% French, 20% Dutch | 74% Sinhala-speakers, 18% Tamil-speakers (13% Sri Lankan Tamils, rest Indian Tamils) |
| **Approach** | **accommodation**: four constitutional amendments (1970–1993) | **majoritarianism**: 1956 Act made Sinhala the only official language |
| **Key measures** | equal Dutch and French ministers; powers to states; equal representation in Brussels; community governments | preferential policies for Sinhala in universities and jobs; the state to protect and foster Buddhism |
| **Result** | unity kept; Brussels chosen as the headquarters of the European Union | alienation of Tamils, demand for Tamil Eelam, civil war (ended 2009) |

blocks.question: In Belgium, which language do 59 per cent of the people speak?
blocks.explanation: 59 per cent live in the Flemish region and speak Dutch.
option_feedback: English is not one of the three groups.

blocks.question: Which 1956 measure in Sri Lanka alienated the Tamils?
options: An Act recognising Sinhala as the only official language
An Act making Tamil the only official language
Equal numbers of ministers from both groups
blocks.explanation: It disregarded Tamil and was part of a series of majoritarian measures.

sections.title: Accommodation in Belgium and why power sharing is desirable

blocks.title: The Belgian model and the case for sharing power
blocks.body:
**Accommodation in Belgium:** the Belgian leaders took a different path. They recognised the existence of **regional differences and cultural diversities**. Between **1970 and 1993**, they **amended their constitution four times** to work out an arrangement that would enable everyone to live together within the same country. The Belgian model:
1. The constitution prescribes that the number of **Dutch and French-speaking ministers shall be equal** in the central government. Some special laws require the support of a **majority of members from each linguistic group**. Thus, no single community can make decisions unilaterally.
2. Many powers of the central government have been given to **state governments** of the two regions. The state governments are **not subordinate** to the central government.
3. **Brussels** has a **separate government** in which both communities have **equal representation**. The French-speaking people accepted equal representation in Brussels because the Dutch-speaking community accepted equal representation in the central government.
4. Apart from the central and state governments, there is a **third kind of government**, the **'community government'**, elected by people belonging to one language community (Dutch, French or German-speaking), no matter where they live. It has power over **cultural, educational and language-related issues**.

The Belgian model is complicated, but it has worked well. It helped **avoid civic strife** and a possible **division of the country on linguistic lines**. When many countries of Europe came together to form the **European Union**, **Brussels** was chosen as its **headquarters**.

**Lessons:** both are democracies, but they dealt with the question of power sharing differently. In Belgium, the leaders realised that the unity of the country is possible only by **respecting the feelings and interests** of different communities. Sri Lanka shows that if a majority community wants to force its dominance over others and refuses to share power, it can **undermine the unity** of the country.

**Why power sharing is desirable:**
- **Prudential reasons** (based on careful calculation of gains and losses): power sharing is good because it helps to **reduce the possibility of conflict** between social groups. Since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, power sharing is a good way to **ensure the stability of the political order**. Imposing the will of the majority over others may look attractive in the short run, but in the long run it undermines the unity of the nation. **Tyranny of the majority** is not just oppressive for the minority; it often brings ruin to the majority as well.
- **Moral reasons** (the intrinsic worth of power sharing): power sharing is the **very spirit of democracy**. A democratic rule involves sharing power with those affected by its exercise, and who have to live with its effects. People have a **right to be consulted** on how they are to be governed. A **legitimate government** is one where citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system.
Prudential reasons stress that power sharing brings **better outcomes**; moral reasons emphasise the very act of power sharing as **valuable in itself**.

blocks.question: What is a 'community government' in Belgium?
options: A government elected by people of one language community, with power over culture, education and language
A government run by village elders
blocks.explanation: It is elected by Dutch, French or German-speaking people, no matter where they live.
option_feedback: The community government is a third kind of government.
Brussels has a separate government with equal representation.
That is not the Belgian model.

blocks.question: 'Power sharing reduces conflict between social groups and ensures political stability.' This is a:
blocks.explanation: Prudential reasons are based on careful calculation of gains and losses.
option_feedback: Moral reasons stress the intrinsic value of power sharing.

blocks.title: Four ways power is shared
blocks.body:
The idea of power sharing has emerged in opposition to the notion of **undivided political power**. For a long time it was believed that all power of a government must reside in one person or group located at one place. Modern democracies share power in many ways:

1. **Horizontal distribution of power (among different organs of government):** power is shared among the **legislature, executive and judiciary**, placed at the same level to exercise different powers. Such separation ensures that none of the organs can exercise **unlimited power**; each organ **checks** the others. This is called a system of **checks and balances**. For example, in India the executive (ministers and officials) exercises power but is **responsible to Parliament or State Assemblies**; similarly, although judges are appointed by the executive, they can **check the functioning of the executive or laws made by legislatures**.
2. **Vertical division of power (among governments at different levels):** a general government for the entire country (the **central or Union government**) and governments at the provincial or regional level (**state governments** in India). Such a general government for the entire country is usually called a **federal government**. The same principle can be extended to levels **lower than the state**, such as the **municipality and panchayat**.
3. **Power shared among different social groups**, such as religious and linguistic groups. **'Community government'** in Belgium is a good example. In some countries there are constitutional and legal arrangements whereby **socially weaker sections and women** are represented in legislatures and administration, like the **reserved constituencies** in India. This gives space to minority communities in the government.
4. **Power shared among political parties, pressure groups and movements:** in a democracy, citizens must have freedom to choose among various contenders for power. **Competition among parties** ensures that power does not remain in one hand; in the long run power is shared among parties that represent different ideologies and social groups. Sometimes this sharing is direct, when two or more parties form an alliance to contest elections and form a **coalition government**. Interest groups such as **traders, businessmen, industrialists, farmers and industrial workers** also share governmental power, through participation in governmental committees or by influencing decision-making.

blocks.title: Forms of power sharing
blocks.body:
| Form of power sharing | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizontal**: among organs of government | legislature, executive and judiciary at the same level; checks and balances | judges check laws made by legislatures |
| **Vertical**: among governments at different levels | union, state and local governments | federal government; panchayats and municipalities |
| **Among social groups** | religious and linguistic groups, weaker sections, women | 'community government' in Belgium; reserved constituencies in India |
| **Among parties, pressure groups and movements** | competition and alliances; influence of interest groups | coalition government; traders, farmers and workers' groups |

blocks.question: Power shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary is called:
blocks.explanation: It creates a system of checks and balances.
option_feedback: Vertical is among levels of government.
That is sharing among social groups.

blocks.question: When two or more parties form an alliance and run the government, it is a:
blocks.explanation: Germany's grand coalition of 2005 is an example.
option_feedback: That is for language communities in Belgium.
Unitary means one main level of government.
Federal refers to levels of government.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Belgium numbers: "59-40-1 and 80-20"**: 59% Dutch (Flemish), 40% French (Wallonia), 1% German; Brussels 80% French, 20% Dutch.
- **Sri Lanka numbers: "74-18-13"**: 74% Sinhala, 18% Tamil, 13% Sri Lankan Tamils.
- **Sri Lanka timeline: 1948 independence → 1956 Sinhala only → 1980s Tamil Eelam demand → civil war ends 2009.**
- **Belgian model: "Equal, States, Brussels, Community"** (equal ministers, powers to states, equal Brussels government, community government).
- **Two reasons: Prudential = Peace (better outcomes); Moral = Meaning of democracy (intrinsic value).**
- **Four forms: "Here Visit Some Parties"** = Horizontal, Vertical, Social groups, Parties.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Swapping the Belgian figures: **59% speak Dutch** (Flemish region), **40% speak French** (Wallonia); in Brussels **80% speak French**.
2. Saying the French speakers were the majority in Belgium: they were the **minority**, but richer and more powerful.
3. Calling the 1956 Act a Tamil language Act: it made **Sinhala the only official language**.
4. Mixing up prudential (better outcomes) and moral (intrinsic value) reasons.
5. Saying horizontal sharing is among levels of government: horizontal is among **organs**; vertical is among **levels**.
6. Saying the Sri Lankan civil war ended in 1983: it ended in **2009**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Divide the class into a 'majority' and a 'minority' group and let them decide the class picnic spot twice: once by a simple majority vote, and once by a rule that needs both groups to agree. Discuss which decision the whole class accepted more happily, and link it to Belgium and Sri Lanka.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Think of your school or housing society. Give one example each of horizontal sharing, vertical sharing and sharing among groups that you can see there.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Belgium and Sri Lanka show two different ways of dealing with diversity.' Compare them in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Belgium recognised regional and cultural differences and amended its constitution four times between 1970 and 1993. It made the number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers equal, gave powers to state governments, set up a separate Brussels government with equal representation, and created community governments for culture, education and language. This accommodation avoided civic strife, kept the country united, and Brussels became the headquarters of the European Union. Sri Lanka followed majoritarianism: the 1956 Act made Sinhala the only official language, Sinhala applicants were favoured for jobs and universities, and the state was to protect Buddhism. Tamils felt alienated, demanded Tamil Eelam, and a civil war followed. Power sharing builds unity; majoritarianism destroys it.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Belgium (59% Dutch, 40% French, 1% German) faced tension because the French-speaking minority was richer and more powerful.
- Sri Lanka (74% Sinhala, 18% Tamil) adopted majoritarian measures after 1948, alienating Tamils and leading to civil war (ended 2009).
- Belgium accommodated diversity through equal ministers, powers to states, an equal Brussels government and community governments.
- Power sharing is desirable for prudential reasons (less conflict, stability) and moral reasons (the spirit of democracy).
- Forms: horizontal (organs), vertical (levels), among social groups, and among parties, pressure groups and movements.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- The 2025-26 sample paper asked which statements about Belgium's ethnic composition are true (1% German; Brussels 80% French, 20% Dutch), identified Germany's 2005 government as a coalition government, and had a 4-mark case study on Sri Lanka and Belgium (Tamil demands, results of majoritarianism, Belgian provisions).
- 3/5-mark favourites: the Belgian model, majoritarianism in Sri Lanka, prudential and moral reasons, forms of power sharing with examples.
- Memorise the exact percentages; options often swap them.

blocks.back: A belief that the majority community should rule a country in whatever way it wants, disregarding the wishes and needs of the minority.

blocks.front: Name the four elements of the Belgian model.
blocks.back: Equal Dutch and French ministers; powers to state governments; an equal Brussels government; community governments.

blocks.front: What is the difference between prudential and moral reasons for power sharing?
blocks.back: Prudential: it brings better outcomes (less conflict, stability). Moral: it is the very spirit of democracy and valuable in itself.
A system in which each organ of government (legislature, executive, judiciary) checks the others, so none has unlimited power.
